question: Why shouldn’t that worry me?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt describes his leadership: empathy, clarity, and purpose.

Many engineering teams he inherited were “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” He focused on removing those barriers: making intent explicit, creating psychological safety so people could speak honestly, and pushing decisions to the people closest to the work. He coached teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, he built balanced teams of engineers, product managers, and UX architects with equal participation and shared accountability. They used pair programming, collaborative coding, retrospectives, and continuous delivery. He also established a “permit to fail” environment through non-punitive post-mortems and low-stakes experiments. Teams applied lessons to subsequent sprints rather than assigning blame.

That approach included taking ownership when delivery went wrong. At **Norfolk Southern**, the client reported rising defects despite near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership in front of the client and account leadership rather than defending the dashboard. A bottom-up audit exposed tests written after the code and backlog stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done.

He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought in TDD experts to work alongside the engineers. Coaching followed an “I do, we do, you do” progression through boot camps, coding katas, and practice learning sessions. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

Across the Cloud Innovation Center, teams accelerated delivery **4x** after adopting lean product and modern engineering practices. His balanced-team work also achieved **zero-defect production code** through iterative development and real-time feedback.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Yes. At **Norfolk Southern**, the working practices Matt introduced did not initially stick.

During the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement in early **2020**, Matt brought in a balanced team and emphasized test-driven development to modernize the Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A couple of months in, the client reported rising defects even though dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The credibility hit landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery. The pandemic was also forcing the team into remote work.

Pairing, test-first development, and continuous integration had been in place from the start, but the follow-up discipline was missing. An engineer was building from his own interpretation rather than the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Vague stories without defined scenarios or a definition of done left room for that to happen. The dashboard looked reassuring while the client kept finding defects.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He opened the codebase and test suite to a bottom-up audit, rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories, and brought in frontend and backend TDD experts to work alongside the engineers.

He then changed the daily reinforcement: rotating pairs, pairing new engineers with seasoned practitioners, and checking test-first work at standup. He also restructured agile rituals to keep stakeholders, developers, and product managers aligned.

The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. After the experts left, pairing and test-first remained the default, and the crisis failure mode did not recur. Matt’s stated lesson was that implementing a practice is the easy half; reinforcement, follow-up, and verification make it real.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Here's a great example.

At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, Matt’s decentralized leadership model did not work as designed at first. The center was designed flat from day one: autonomy at the team level, collective ownership, and minimal middle layers. But many practitioners came from legacy delivery organizations where top-down, command-and-control patterns were the norm.

Those habits reasserted themselves. Decisions drifted upward, teams waited for direction, and bottlenecks formed where autonomy was supposed to be. Designing the model was not the same as living it. Converting people to the model took enforcement and revalidation, multiple times, and the path was bumpy.

Matt’s response was to change how decisions were handled in everyday work, rather than rely on the flat structure alone. He established cross-functional teams of product managers, designers, and engineers with shared ownership and decision-making authority. Anchors and team leads were expected to remove obstacles rather than control outcomes. He also created clear, flexible guidelines for decentralized decisions, tied to project objectives, and used continuous retrospectives so teams could adjust based on feedback.

The account reports that bottlenecks were removed and teams consistently met project milestones. It does not provide a quantified recovery timeline or describe a case where Matt ultimately abandoned the model.

So this is an example of his approach failing to take hold initially, followed by repeated intervention, not a documented example of an unsuccessful final outcome.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed—and what happened afterward.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization delivery for a **Fortune 500** financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with existing documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. Instead of verifying those controls, he assumed they were correct. He relied on inherited documentation, did not audit who could trigger downstream jobs or email processes, and did not implement compensating controls such as data masking or email interception. He also did not verify whether production customer names and email addresses had been scrubbed from downstream environments.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed, then worked collectively to implement corrective controls. The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project—a systemic failure with an individual consequence.

Matt’s stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership became day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach.

question: What did he change afterward?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s the payments work Matt has done.

At **JP Morgan Chase**, Matt was Technology Delivery Lead for the payment engine behind ACCESS Next Generation. The bank needed more than Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries offered out of the box: its **135,000+** clients across **180+** countries required distinct payment formatting, validation, compliance, and workflows. Regional legacy systems also had different data models, client configurations, and entitlement structures that had to be consolidated without interrupting live payments.

Matt managed a blended team of **40+** across Mumbai, Bangalore, and the US, spending **70-80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices. He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and government tax payment modules, alongside Message Authentication Code security, payment-type-specific entitlements, sanctions screening, and real-time global reporting. He also led payments data migration, preserving compliance traceability and maintaining uninterrupted payment operations. ACCESS launched in **April 2011** as the bank’s unified global corporate banking portal.

At **American Express**, his work focused on adoption of the Virtual Payments Platform, which was replacing a legacy mainframe system. Clients lacked SDKs, usable documentation, and a sandbox; dependency bottlenecks also delayed testing. Matt co-created a developer portal, developed Java, .NET, and Python SDKs, and built a secure sandbox with refreshed client data. He introduced environment virtualization, Lean Product and XP practices, and a Client Onboarding Test Drive. API consumption and trial usage increased within **3 months** of relaunch, onboarding time declined, and the portal team delivered over **261** additional story points of customer-focused value.

At **RBC**, Matt designed cross-border payment workflows from initiation through settlement and reconciliation. He defined real-time FX integration, automated alerts, recurring payments, Interac e-Transfer workflows, and batch processing. The deliverable was a complete implementation blueprint ready for development execution; revised payment cutoff processes reduced wire transfer delays and improved SLA compliance.

Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose. In teams he inherited, engineers were often “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” At **Accenture’s** Cloud Innovation Center, a rigid hierarchical culture also made people slow to share ideas. Some teams avoided risks because they feared blame, which slowed delivery and kept them from experimenting with new engineering practices.

Matt pushed decisions to the people closest to the work, made intent explicit, and used transparency, direct feedback, and open communication. He brought product managers, designers, and engineers together in balanced teams, delivering thin-slice, production-ready solutions so they could get user feedback rather than wait for a large release.

He established weekly brainstorming sessions where ideas were considered without judgment. Recognition focused on contributions that advanced shared project goals rather than individual accolades. Team members began sharing ideas more freely and identifying more efficient ways to reach project milestones.

His “permit to fail” environment included non-punitive post-mortems and lean, low-stakes experiments. Instead of pointing fingers, teams examined mistakes and applied the lessons to subsequent sprints, preventing recurrence of identified failure patterns. In early-stage product work, he set expectations that prototypes and user tests would sometimes fail, then used those results to shape product direction week by week.

Alongside that environment, Matt grounded engineering work in automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first practices. At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. Teams experimented more freely, repeat errors declined, and delivery timelines shortened.

question: What’s his leadership style?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s an example from **Norfolk Southern**.

During the Cloud Innovation Center’s first major engagement in **2020**, Matt’s team was modernizing **Norfolk Southern’s** legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform. A few months in, as the pandemic forced everyone into remote work, the client reported rising defects. The dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The concerns landed in front of both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He investigated and found an engineer was building from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. Coverage looked complete, but defects went undetected. The backlog also lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Matt ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly. He rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories and brought frontend and backend test-driven development experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team. They redid the code and test cases, writing tests before the code they tested.

Instead of stopping at new process rules, he introduced hands-on Samman-style coaching: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing engineers with subject-matter experts through an “I do, we do, you do” progression. He also restructured agile ceremonies and provided product management and story-writing training.

Defect rates dropped, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. Client and account leadership confidence returned through the open audit and visible improvements.

Matt’s payments work included building the payment engine and global gateway for **JP Morgan Chase**’s ACCESS platform, migrating legacy payment systems, and improving developer integration for **American Express**’s Virtual Payments Platform.

answer_md:
🐾 Tracking this down...

At **Norfolk Southern**, Matt’s first major Cloud Innovation Center engagement ran into a quality crisis. The team was modernizing a legacy Revenue and Shipment Planning platform in **2020**. A couple of months in, as the pandemic moved work remote, the client reported rising defects even though the dashboards showed near-complete test coverage. The concerns reached both the client and **Accenture** account leadership, who were already accustomed to waterfall delivery.

Matt took ownership of the failure rather than defending the metrics. He ran a bottom-up audit of the codebase and test suite and showed the gaps openly. An engineer had been working from his own interpretation instead of the backlog story, then writing tests after the code. The backlog was also part of the problem: stories lacked defined scenarios and a definition of done.

Matt rebuilt the backlog with SMART, testable stories. Instead of simply telling engineers to follow test-driven development, he brought frontend and backend TDD experts from Columbus to work side by side with the team, then had the code and test cases redone properly.

He used the Samman coaching approach: boot camps, coding katas, practice learning sessions, and pairing engineers with subject-matter experts through an “I do, we do, you do” progression. He also delivered product management and SMART story training and restructured agile ceremonies to keep stakeholders, developers, and product managers working from the same requirements.

Defect rates dropped as story quality and test-first discipline took hold. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see, and client and account-leadership confidence was restored through the open audit and visible improvement.

question: How long did that take?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s how Matt built and scaled the organization.

The CIC growth story starts with a **10-person pilot**, rather than **4**, and reaches **150+ practitioners** across engineering, architecture, product, and design over **4 years**. At **Accenture**, growing client demand required new Cloud Innovation Centers in Atlanta and Tampa. Many hires lacked hands-on cloud-native or Agile experience. Matt had to build hiring, development, evaluation, and promotion processes without adding layers of management.

He built a hiring engine across bench searches, campus recruiting, contract-to-hire, and job requisitions. Georgia Tech recruiting, hackathons, and job fairs expanded the talent pipeline. Instead of relying only on interviews, engineers completed hands-on TDD pairing auditions; product managers and designers worked through live scoping exercises. Matt held the closing interview and made every final hiring decision. During scaling pushes, the process produced **4-6 net-new practitioners per week**, with interview participation capped at **2 slots per practitioner per week** to protect delivery.

Hiring was followed by structured enablement, tailored to skill gaps, and round-robin pairing with seasoned practitioners. Teams progressed through “I do, we do, you do” toward independent delivery. Senior engineers coached junior colleagues, while peer-led tech talks, skills matrices, and career development sessions continued learning inside client work. Pair programming, TDD, CI/CD, user research, and Build-Measure-Learn became standard working practices.

Matt kept the organization deliberately flat, with **11-13 practice and client leads** reporting directly to him. Balanced teams held execution power; experienced engineering anchors kept leads informed without adding middle management. Monday allocation reviews assigned practitioners across engagements and internal learning tracks. Performance evaluations drew on recent pair partners, product managers, and anchors, rather than a manager’s impressions.

The organization reached **150+ practitioners**, with near-zero attrition in the first **2 years**. Across the CIC delivery model, **10-person balanced teams** delivered equivalent output to traditional **20-person teams**, with **4X faster velocity** and zero-defect deployments. question: Can I see his résumé?

answer_md:
🐾 Found it! Matt was brought in roughly seven months into **Fiserv**'s 14-month, **$8.5M** white-label card portal program, the shared platform behind branded credit card sites for **2M+** cardholders across **15** financial institutions. The **45-person** globally dispersed team had missed multiple consecutive deadlines, and client stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation. He recovered a Q4 release that was **3 weeks** behind, avoiding **$500K** in penalties, and the program was delivered **3%** under budget with zero critical defects at launch.

Want to hear how he moved that team from 6-month waterfall releases to 2-week sprints?

🐾 Here’s how Matt changed the delivery cycle.

At **Fiserv**, the **45-person** team was working through **6-month** waterfall release cycles, with requirements buried in **200-page** business requirements documents organized by system modules. Developers in India, testers in the Philippines, and designers in Ireland had no visibility into work status. Deadlines kept slipping, client stakeholders were threatening contract cancellation, and PMO and compliance teams resisted the move to agile.

Matt changed how work was defined and tracked. He decomposed the requirements into persona-based user stories and rebuilt JIRA from a single To Do/Done board into a multi-tiered Kanban/Scrum architecture. The program’s **47** acceptance criteria became Epics, with user stories moving through specific workflow columns.

He established follow-the-sun synchronization: **7 AM CST** scrum-of-scrums for offshore-to-onshore handoffs and **11 PM CST** syncs for the return handoff. Bi-weekly sprint demos brought branding, UI, and ADA compliance decisions forward instead of leaving them until month **6**. When stakeholders lacked bandwidth for regular feedback, he negotiated dedicated review windows so work would not stall.

Matt maintained steering committee reporting while adding sprint-level visibility. For PMO and compliance, he used JIRA as the system of record, with audit trails, attached ADA scans, and developer comments rather than static Word documents. He also coached offshore teams on empowerment over command-and-control and built JAWS/NVDA screen reader audits into the Definition of Done.

Alongside those changes, he replaced SVN with Git/GitHub, required senior-developer code reviews and unit tests, and introduced Hudson CI with SonarQube and JUnit quality gates.

The team adopted **2-week** sprints within **3 months**. JIRA gave **50+** stakeholders across **3** time zones real-time visibility, and PMO and compliance accepted it as the system of record. Production deployments moved from less than once per month to weekly-to-monthly cycles—not a production release every sprint.

Matt led **Norfolk Southern’s** Revenue and Shipment Planning modernization as a Director at **Accenture**, on the Cloud Innovation Center’s first engagement. Core scheduling, billing, and order-to-cash ran on a mainframe dating to the **1970s**. Orders could disappear unnoticed until customers called, business rules lived in COBOL and assembly maintained by a shrinking workforce, and clerks manually handled waybill and rating fallout. Modernization had to happen without stopping the railroad, while client teams worked through mainframe thinking, account leadership expected waterfall delivery, and the pandemic forced remote work.

Matt led domain-driven design and event storming to map business functions, data flows, and dependencies. The mainframe remained the system of record while APIs, microservices, and CockroachDB grew alongside it. Change data capture synchronized the platforms; reconciliation checked that nothing was lost. His team incrementally replaced components using the Strangler pattern, API gateways, and anti-corruption layers rather than a wholesale cutover. The scope extended across order management, booking, credit, service fulfillment, planning, billing, and accounts receivable. Architecture work also included the Boris Exercise and SNAP-E documentation.

When the client grew restless for tangible progress, Matt brought revenue management into the innovation hub to co-create the Shipper Revenue System interface, from personas to high-fidelity prototypes in weekly build-measure-learn iterations. He also confronted rising defects despite near-complete test coverage: auditing code and tests, rebuilding vague backlog stories, and bringing in TDD experts for hands-on coaching.

For client enablement, he designed a **2-day** CIC Academy course delivered **twice a month** over **6 months**. Pairing rotated scarce domain knowledge through teams, while client contributors learned Angular, Node, Spring Boot, and cloud-native practices.

The engagement scaled to **3 balanced teams** and began transitioning **1 team** to Monterrey. The MVP covered **95%** of targeted use cases, capturing real orders with clean data feeding the mainframe. EDI validation caught fallout proactively and notified trading partners instead of waiting for customer calls. The client team was co-creating in weekly iterations, and the client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see.

Matt worked on **RBC’s** Day**2Day** Corporate Banking modernization as a Senior Technology Architecture Manager at **Accenture**. The bank was evaluating Bottomline WebSeries as the payment hub engine to replace **RBC Express**. Existing systems had performance and scalability limitations and lacked digital offerings. The question was whether the proposed platform could meet the bank’s requirements before further investment.

Matt conducted an architecture assessment and gap/fit analysis rather than proceeding directly into implementation. He scored Data, Application, Technology, and Business Architecture maturity, reviewed code and documentation, and interviewed stakeholders. Drawing on prior WebSeries implementation experience, he created architectural heat maps and target-system models with a cost-to-fix versus benefit comparison. The assessment found that WebSeries lacked the modularity **RBC** needed for its long-term digital operating model. The bank redirected technical resources toward higher-priority initiatives before significant spend was committed.

He also established the PMO during discovery and requirements. Beyond status reporting, he introduced designated team contacts, shared real-time updates, daily summaries, and a task-tracking matrix to clarify assignments and prevent duplicate work. The communication framework eliminated missed program updates.

When the previous data conversion lead left, Matt took over the workstream from scratch. He analyzed legacy payment records, documented source-to-target transformation rules, planned mock conversion cycles, and established reconciliation checks for payment amounts and beneficiary details. He delivered the end-to-end conversion plan and coordinated business, IT, vendor, onshore, and offshore teams.

Other work addressed mobile readiness and reporting limitations. Matt defined API integration points, cheque deposit requirements, and cross-device scalability needs. Corporate clients could access only **180 days** of transaction and chargeback history, while audit teams needed up to **7 years**. He delivered requirements and solution designs for scheduled reporting, scalable exports, and extended historical access, plus client enablement materials. These were blueprints and planning deliverables, not a claim that a replacement platform had launched.
